name: Sam Weber

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Sam, thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or political parties. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Could you start by telling me a bit about yourself?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sam, 27. I live with my partner Lena, she's a teaching assistant at the primary school round the corner. We rent a semi near the football ground, and I help coach the under-elevens at the club on Saturdays. I left school at sixteen, worked on building sites, then got into the warehouse about a year ago because my cousin vouched for me. We've saved well, probably eight months of bills, and I've got a van I own outright.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And what does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm at a drinks distributor, so it's cases of beer, soft drinks, crisps, that sort of thing, going out to pubs and corner shops. I pick with a voice headset that tells me the aisle and the number of cases, and I say a check number back. It's heavy and repetitive, and I'm still slower than the lads who've been there years, especially when the mixed orders come in. I like the banter and that it keeps me fit. What gets me is the Friday before a bank holiday when every pub wants double.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Wouldn't surprise me. Every few years something's going to change the world.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, let people get on with their jobs. I'd say it at the club bar, probably. I don't really post online, maybe in the lads' group chat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think it's fine for me. I use the chatbot sometimes for car problems or to write an email to the council, but that's it. My job stays and our savings grow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and keep saving. I'd probably go for the HGV mechanic apprenticeship my brother did, in a year or two, because it's a proper trade with good money. And Lena and I would think about getting married.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Content, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What draws you to the mechanic apprenticeship?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My brother Tom did it, and he's never been out of work in ten years. I like seeing someone go first and do well before I jump. Lorries always need fixing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there any pressure on you, even in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My back and knees, a bit, from the cases. Not now, but in ten years. That's partly why the trade appeals.

I'd say it at the **club bar** rather than online.
think: It's **fine for me**: I use a chatbot only for car problems and emails.
My **job stays** and our savings keep growing.
do: Go for an **HGV mechanic apprenticeship** in a year or two.

fieldNote: His **brother's path** into a trade is his blueprint.
He thinks about his **body** wearing out more than about AI.
A **steady** man: he moves once someone close has proved it works.

Apply for an HGV mechanic apprenticeship in a year or two

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The office side, then. Ordering and planning. We're mostly lifting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say change is normal, you get on with it. I'd tell the young lads to get a trade. I'm not one to moan about companies doing what's good for business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'm all right in the warehouse for a good while. The voice headset already tells me what to do, so the thinking bit's mostly done by computers anyway. The lifting is still us. But I'd want to be in a trade before robots get good at lifting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the mechanic apprenticeship within the year, once I'd talked to my brother about the best place. I'd keep the savings up, because apprentice pay is lower to start. I'd probably try the AI tools they use for diagnosing engines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. It doesn't feel like it's coming for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the lower apprentice pay be a problem?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. Lena's wage plus our savings would cover the gap for a couple of years. We'd cut back on holidays, but that's fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gary in the transport office, who plans the routes. He's fifty-odd and that's exactly what computers do. I'd feel for him, but that's how it goes.

I'd tell young colleagues to **get a trade**.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years? And robots by 2031. That's quicker than I'd like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's happening, so we need to look after each other. I'd tell people to get into a trade fast. I wouldn't be angry, I'd be practical.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think my warehouse job's done by 2031. Even the mechanic trade might shrink after robots come, though fixing a lorry on a roadside in the rain seems far off for a robot. I'd worry about Lena too, if AI can teach kids.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the apprenticeship straight away, before everyone else has the same idea. I'd save harder, maybe put off the wedding a year. And I'd talk to my brother about whether we could start our own small repair business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd have a plan, but it's moving fast and I'd be racing against it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why put off the wedding?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because weddings cost a fortune, and I'd want the money there if things go wrong. Lena would understand. We'd still get married, just a bit later and smaller.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you lean on anyone if it went badly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Family first, my brother and my parents. Not the government, if I can help it. I'd rather work for less than take handouts.

I'd tell people to **get into a trade** fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2031 then 2034 for robots. That's a bit better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to sort yourself out, so do it. I'd tell the lads at the club to think about trades. I'd keep it practical.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think this is enough time for me to be a qualified mechanic before the robots come. My warehouse job would go, but I'd be gone first. I'd still worry a bit for Lena.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the apprenticeship within a year and finish by 2030. I'd keep working weekends at the warehouse if they'd let me. We'd get married as planned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not for me so much, more for people around me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would worry you for Lena?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If AI can teach reading and maths, schools might need fewer assistants. She's good with the kids who struggle, though. I'd hope that stays human.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you try AI tools more in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Once I'm in the garage, yeah, if the older mechanics are using them. I'd follow their lead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, robots in 2039. Plenty of time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say no one has an excuse not to be ready. I'd tell the young lads at football to learn a trade. That's my answer for most things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd think I'm sorted. Mechanic trade, married, maybe a kid or two. I'd keep an eye on it, but I wouldn't lose sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the apprenticeship in the next couple of years, without rushing. We'd get married and start a family. I'd keep saving, maybe buy a house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, just a little. More for the young ones I coach than for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the boys you coach?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the boys I coach to learn a trade they can do with their hands and not to be scared of the computer side. And to turn up on time. That never goes out of fashion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could go wrong in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Everyone relaxing because it's ten years off, then it's on top of them. I'd try not to be one of those.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because it's racing. What would help is apprenticeships that adults can afford, with decent pay, and employers taking on people in their late twenties, not just school leavers.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the trades. Everyone talks about computers, but someone still has to fix the lorry when it breaks down on the motorway.

headlineQuote: Everyone talks about computers, but someone still has to fix the lorry when it breaks down on the motorway.
portrait: Sam is a **27-year-old picker** at a drinks distributor, living with **Lena**, a teaching assistant.
He coaches **under-elevens** football and owns his van outright.
He follows his brother's lead into an **HGV mechanic apprenticeship**, the centre of every plan.
Fast AGI makes him **anxious** and delay the wedding; slower change leaves him uneasy for others.
He'd rely on **family**, not government, and wants paid adult apprenticeships.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because he'd be **racing** to retrain.
